questions.question: Compare the ideas of Democritus and Dalton about atoms. State four points of Dalton's atomic theory and explain which point has been modified.
questions.expected_answer: Democritus (about 400 BCE) argued that matter could not be divided for ever and must consist of uncuttable particles, atomos, but this was reasoning without experimental evidence and was rejected by Aristotle. Dalton (1803) based his theory on measurements showing that elements combine in fixed proportions by mass. Points: all matter is made of atoms; atoms of the same element are identical, and atoms of different elements differ; atoms cannot be created or destroyed in chemical reactions; atoms combine in simple whole-number ratios to form compounds; reactions rearrange atoms. Modified: atoms can be split by nuclear processes and contain smaller particles; atoms of the same element can differ in mass (isotopes) because of different numbers of neutrons.

questions.question: An atom is about 0.1 nm across. Show how many atoms fit across a 0.5 mm full stop, and explain why atoms cannot be seen with a light microscope but can be imaged today.
questions.expected_answer: 0.5 mm = 0.5 × 10⁻³ m and 0.1 nm = 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m, so 0.5 × 10⁻³ ÷ 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ = 5 × 10⁶, about 5 million atoms. Atoms are far smaller than the wavelength of visible light (about 400 to 700 nm), so a light microscope cannot resolve them. A scanning tunnelling microscope moves an extremely fine tip across a surface and measures a tiny electric current, mapping individual atoms; in 1989 IBM researchers arranged 35 xenon atoms to spell the company name.

questions.question: Explain, in terms of atoms, what an element is, giving examples of elements whose atoms are single, joined in pairs and packed in a lattice. Use the alphabet analogy to explain how about ninety kinds of atom make millions of substances.
questions.expected_answer: An element is a substance made of only one kind of atom, so it cannot be broken down into simpler substances by chemical means. Single atoms: helium, neon, argon. Pairs (diatomic molecules): oxygen, nitrogen, hydrogen, chlorine. Lattice: metals such as iron and copper; diamond. Like 26 letters combining into hundreds of thousands of words, about ninety natural kinds of atom combine in different numbers and arrangements into compounds; for example carbon, hydrogen and oxygen form sugar, starch, cellulose, fats and alcohol. In reactions atoms are rearranged, not destroyed or changed into other elements.
